title: Osiris Reference
subtitle: Language semantics, built-in functions, modules, I/O, and native integration design.

sections.title: What Osiris is
sections.summary: Osiris is a deterministic, inspectable language for exact math, text transforms, data pipelines, and module loading.
paragraphs: Osiris keeps the core language small while giving the runtime enough structure to understand modules, exports, numeric exactness, tensors, and the build pipeline.
The language is designed to be readable, testable, and useful for math-heavy work without turning every program into a framework.
When the language needs to grow, it grows around the visible pipeline: input, transform, inspect, and output.

cards.title: Guiding rule
cards.text: Prefer explicit data flow, explicit module boundaries, and explicit numeric intent.

cards.title: Default numeric model
cards.text: The default literal type remains `number`, while specialized constructors handle exact, wide, packed, `tensor`, and fixed-precision forms.

cards.title: Control flow
cards.text: `if`, `while`, `for`, `match`, `switch`, `try`/`catch`, `return`, `break`, and `continue` make the core language expressive without hiding the flow of computation.

cards.title: Native build
cards.text: Osiris lowers a tested subset through C so the resulting executable evaluates program logic at runtime. Coverage is feature-specific; see the backend support matrix before depending on native compilation.

sections.title: Language semantics
sections.summary: Programs are statement lists with lexical scope, explicit imports, exact math where possible, and controlled output through `emit`.
paragraphs: A file is normally a list of statements separated by newlines or semicolons. The usual shape is `package`, `export`, `import`, `macro`, `let`, and `emit`, but that order is a convention rather than a law.

Values are inspected through the runtime rather than hidden behind magic. The runtime preserves exactness, width metadata, tensor shape, module identity, and other structural information wherever it can.
Imports are alias-based and version-aware. File modules, `std` modules, and local module graphs are resolved explicitly, and the loader records manifests for repeatable builds.

Ordinary expressions execute in source order and synchronous `emit` statements append values in production order. Tasks make concurrency explicit through `spawn`, `await`, `parallel`, `cancel`, and `timeout`; concurrent bodies return values instead of emitting, and file and data helpers remain deliberately visible host operations.

cards.title: Scoping
cards.text: `let` introduces lexical bindings. Shadowing is allowed, and loop-local state is carried forward by the execution model when needed.

cards.title: Control flow
cards.text: `if`, `while`, `for`, `return`, `break`, `continue`, `match`, `switch`, and `try`/`catch` are the visible control-flow tools.

cards.title: Exactness
cards.text: Exact operands stay exact where possible, including rational division and wide integer exponentiation.

cards.title: Modules
cards.text: Module imports are explicit, version selectors are supported, and exported names are the public contract.

cards.title: Output stream
cards.text: `emit` writes values into the program output stream in execution order, which makes the observable result of a script easy to reason about and easy to test.

cards.title: Error propagation
cards.text: Use `try`/`catch` for explicit handling and the postfix `?` operator for early propagation from fallible expressions when you want the current function to return the failure directly.

cards.title: Scope-bound cleanup
cards.text: Use `defer { ... }` immediately after acquiring an owned resource. Actions execute once in LIFO order on every synchronous or task exit, and `close` also dispatches to a user-defined zero-argument closable method.

cards.title: Blocking I/O
cards.text: I/O is host-backed and explicit. Use `read`, `write`, `readbytes`, `csv`, `jsonparse`, `lines`, and stream handles for visible file/data flow; task-aware behavior is documented with each API.

cards.title: Memory management
cards.text: Osiris values are managed by the host runtime. Source programs do not allocate or free memory manually, and the runtime leans on Go-managed storage for temporary objects, module state, and evaluation artifacts.

cards.title: Garbage collection
cards.text: There is no user-facing garbage collector to tune. Lifetime is governed by the host runtime's collector and the shape of the current evaluation graph, so programmers focus on data flow instead of manual reclamation.

cards.title: Hosted runtime and native boundary
cards.text: The interpreter and VM are Go-hosted: streams, task state, and temporary buffers use host-managed memory. `defer` supplies deterministic lexical cleanup and `close` is idempotent for built-in handles; neither is a garbage-collector finalizer. The ahead-of-time C backend has explicit cleanup edges for its supported executable subset, while host-backed streams, networking, and asynchronous I/O remain compile-time native boundaries.

sections.title: Writing Osiris programs
sections.summary: Write programs as explicit, deterministic pipelines: input, named transforms, and output.
paragraphs: Source files normally use the `.osr` extension. Statements are separated by newlines or semicolons; both `//` and `#` introduce line comments.

The readable default order is `package`, `export`, `import`, `macro`, `let`, and `emit`. It is a convention, not a restriction: use functions for named repeated work, loops for iteration, and `match` or `switch` for shape-driven branches.
Keep module surfaces narrow, name intermediate transforms, distinguish text from bytes, and leave output visible. Good Osiris code should be easy to trace when read later.

cards.title: Program shape
cards.text: Put `package` metadata and `export` declarations first when a file is importable; use alias-based `import` declarations and finish with a visible `emit` when practical.

cards.title: Data flow
cards.text: Prefer `read` → transform → `write`. Use `bytes` and fixed-width conversions for binary work instead of treating strings as hidden numbers.

cards.title: Tools
cards.text: Use `fmt`, `run`, `vm`, `trace`, `debug`, `infer`, `ir`, `ssa`, `cfg`, and `deps` to make program behavior and compiler analysis inspectable.

sections.title: Error model
sections.summary: Errors are structured values with stable kinds, public metadata, optional causes, and redaction rules that keep sensitive data out of normal output.
paragraphs: Osiris treats recoverable failures as structured error records instead of plain strings. The runtime preserves the error kind, message, source location, stack frames, and public metadata whenever those details are available.
The public surface is intentionally small and machine-readable. The standard helpers let code create, wrap, inspect, redact, and serialize errors without having to parse error text.

Errors are immutable records. When a program adds context, it gets a new record back instead of mutating the original failure. That keeps error propagation predictable across function boundaries, tasks, and native wrappers.

cards.title: Base model
cards.text: An Osiris error is a structured runtime record with a stable kind/code, a user-facing message, and optional cause, source, stack, metadata, and severity fields. The record is immutable, comparable by structure, and safe to serialize.

cards.title: Taxonomy
cards.text: The standard kinds stay intentionally small: `InvalidArgument`, `NotFound`, `AlreadyExists`, `PermissionDenied`, `Unauthenticated`, `Unavailable`, `Timeout`, `Cancelled`, `Conflict`, `ResourceExhausted`, `OutOfMemory`, `OutOfRange`, `Unsupported`, `NotImplemented`, `ParseError`, `TypeError`, `EncodingError`, `IOError`, `NetworkError`, `DatabaseError`, `InternalError`, and `UnknownError`.

cards.title: Metadata
cards.text: Public metadata covers `operation`, `resource`, `retryability`, `severity`, `user_message`, `correlation_id`, `component`, `remediation`, `source`, `location`, `timestamp`, and any extra public key/value pairs. Debug metadata is kept separate so sensitive details do not leak into ordinary output.

cards.title: Debug data
cards.text: Debug-only metadata is stored separately so the normal display path and serialized form do not leak sensitive details unless the caller explicitly asks for them. The `redact` helper strips stack details and debug-only state while preserving the public cause chain.

cards.title: Helpers
cards.text: Use `error`, `wrap`, `cause`, `unwrap`, `withmeta`, `withdebug`, `errmeta`, and `redact` to create, inspect, and sanitize error records. `matches` and `is` are the standard kind checks, while `try`/`catch` handles recoverable failures explicitly.

cards.title: Result and option
cards.text: `Result` values use `ok` and `err` constructors. `Option` values use `some` and `none`. `unwrap` extracts payloads, `expect` attaches a user-facing failure, `or_else` supplies a fallback value, `map`/`map_error`/`flat_map` transform fallible computations lazily, and the postfix `?` operator propagates a recoverable failure to the current function boundary.

cards.title: Fatal errors
cards.text: `panic`, `trap`, and `assert` raise fatal structured errors. They are treated as unrecoverable, bypass ordinary `catch` handling, and are intended for impossible states rather than expected branching.

cards.title: Boundaries
cards.text: Parser errors, runtime errors, task errors, and native host errors are normalized into structured Osiris errors before they leave the runtime. The same record model is preserved across task boundaries and native wrappers so logging and redaction remain consistent.

sections.title: Tasks, cancellation, and streams
sections.summary: Explicit structured concurrency and host-backed streaming I/O with defined result and output-ordering contracts.
paragraphs: Task behavior is explicit. `spawn` starts a task from one expression, `await` waits for its result, `cancel` requests cooperative cancellation, `parallel` evaluates a fixed ordered group, `race`/`select` choose the first completed branch, and `timeout` evaluates one expression under an integer-millisecond deadline.

Ordinary `run` uses goroutines for task and `parallel` work. The runtime's task-debug mode executes scheduler work deterministically for inspection and tests; programs must not depend on wall-clock completion order in either mode.

Stream handles are explicit blocking file operations. `openread`/`openwrite` create handles; `readline`/`readchunk` and `writechunk` perform the visible I/O; `flush` and `close` complete it. Register `defer { close(handle) }` immediately after acquisition when the handle belongs to the current scope. Use the `*_async` wrappers only when a task value is required.

cards.title: spawn and await
cards.text: `spawn` returns a task immediately. `await` is the suspension point and either returns the task value or propagates the task error/cancellation.

cards.title: cancel
cards.text: `cancel` returns `true` only when cancellation was newly requested; `await` then reports cancellation. Cancellation is cooperative and is observed at runtime safe points such as loop evaluation and task waits.

cards.title: parallel and deterministic results
cards.text: Branches may compute concurrently and result positions retain argument order. Branches cannot use `emit`; return their values and emit the resulting list from the synchronous caller. A branch error cancels sibling work and propagates the failure.

cards.title: race and select
cards.code:
let winner = race(first(), second())
let indexed = select(first(), second())
cards.text: `race` returns the first completed branch value. `select` returns `[source_index, value]`, where the index is `u64`. Candidates cannot use `emit`; sibling work is cancelled cooperatively, and deterministic task-debug mode chooses the first source branch.

cards.title: timeout
cards.text: The duration is a non-negative integer number of milliseconds. `timeout` returns the body result if it finishes before the deadline, otherwise it fails with `timeout`. It does not turn a blocking host call into nonblocking I/O; cancellation is cooperative.

cards.title: task-aware I/O
cards.text: Async wrappers return tasks; their I/O work begins in the spawned task and errors propagate through `await`. Use `openread`/`readline`/`readchunk` for explicit incremental streaming.

cards.title: deterministic mode
cards.text: Runtime task-debug mode is an embedding/tooling control, not source syntax. It runs scheduler work deterministically and records task trace events. It preserves source-visible values and argument-ordered results; it is for debugging and validation, not a performance mode.

sections.title: Native interop and build flow
sections.summary: Osiris is becoming a general ahead-of-time compiler with portable C as its first native backend; hosted FFI has a capability-gated, digest-pinned v1 subset.
paragraphs: The native build path lowers a tested `AST`/`IR` subset into readable C whose executable evaluates program logic at runtime, then uses the system C compiler for native code generation. Unsupported operations are rejected during compilation; there is no compile-time execution fallback. The machine-checked backend inventory records every registered builtin, context builtin, language construct, and exported standard-library member with its VM/native status and evidence.
Build a standalone executable with `osiris build -o output program.osr`.

C is the first backend because it is inspectable, portable, and lets mature toolchains handle instruction selection, register allocation, linking, and target-specific optimization. The backend support matrix names the supported subset and its evidence; native parity and measured performance are required before claims of C-level speed.

C libraries are the first native interop target. FFI manifests are digest-pinned and capability-gated before hosted, VM, or generated-C execution. The shared generated-C parity slice covers declared scalar, float, string, constant, immutable-buffer, and mutable-buffer calls; hosted and VM also expose fixed-layout records, opaque handles, and scoped synchronous callbacks with deterministic cleanup.
Go-backed `std` modules already use a host-wrapper pattern: Osiris imports a named module supplied by the Go runtime, not arbitrary Go source at runtime.

cards.title: C libraries
cards.text: Use explicit wrappers and build-time linking for native libraries such as `libm`, `libc`-style helpers, codecs, databases, or math backends.

cards.title: Go host modules
cards.text: Wrap Go code into Osiris-shaped modules instead of trying to dynamically import arbitrary Go packages.

types.name: number
types.summary: Default floating numeric type; unsuffixed integer literals use `u64`.

types.name: complex
types.summary: Complex numeric type with real and imaginary parts; explicit `f32` and `f64` component families are retained.

types.name: interval
types.summary: Exact `interval` with lower and upper bounds.

types.name: simd
types.summary: Fixed-width numeric or boolean lane vector with explicit lane count and element family.

types.name: quat
types.summary: Four-component quaternion with deterministic Hamilton multiplication, conjugation, norm, inverse, and division.

types.name: dual
types.summary: First-order `dual` number for scalar automatic differentiation; native lowering is not yet available.

types.name: sparse_matrix
types.summary: Canonical two-dimensional sparse matrix with deterministic duplicate summation, zero elision, and CSR/CSC format metadata.

types.name: sparse_tensor
types.summary: Canonical n-dimensional COO sparse tensor with explicit shape, coordinate ordering, duplicate summation, and zero elision.

types.name: poly
types.summary: Normalized polynomial whose coefficient family is retained through arithmetic, evaluation, indexing, and codecs.

types.name: future
types.summary: Portable runtime envelope used for the explicit `poly`, `quat`, `simd`, `sparse_matrix`, and `sparse_tensor` value families; programs should use the concrete family types.

groups.title: Core language constructs
groups.summary: The syntax that shapes programs, modules, statements, and control flow.

items.name: package
items.summary: Declare the identity of a file module.
details: Package declarations belong at the top of files that are meant to be imported.
The optional version becomes part of the module contract and can be selected by import selectors.

items.name: export
items.summary: Expose only the listed bindings from a file module.
details: Exports are explicit so imported modules have a stable public surface.
Everything else remains internal to the module unless exported.

items.name: import
items.summary: Load a file module or a std module and bind it to an alias.
details: Imports are always aliased.
Version selectors are supported for both local and `std` modules.
`std` modules are backed by the host runtime, while file modules are parsed and executed as Osiris source.

items.name: const
items.summary: Introduce an immutable compile-time or module-level constant.
details: The initializer may use literals, earlier constants, pure unary/binary operations, lists, or tuples.
Calls, I/O, tasks, runtime-dependent values, mutable bindings, and later assignments are rejected.

items.name: let
items.summary: Introduce a lexical binding.
details: Bindings are scoped to the surrounding block or file and are initialized once at runtime.
Shadowing is allowed and is used deliberately throughout the language.

items.name: var
items.summary: Introduce a mutable local cell and replace its value explicitly.
details: Only `var` locals may be assigned. `let`, `const`, parameters, imports, struct fields, and collection indexes remain immutable.
`var` is contextual so the statistical `var(...)` builtin remains available in expression position.
items.example:
var count = 0
count = count + 1
emit count

items.name: func
items.summary: Define a lexical function with optional checked parameter and result types.
details: Write annotations after parameter names and after the closing parenthesis, without a colon. `func(u32) string` is the exact type of a callable that accepts `u32` and returns `string`.
Functions can use an expression body after `=>` or a block with explicit `return` and a tail expression.
Captured variables are resolved through lexical scope, not dynamic lookup. Recursive and mutually recursive signatures are checked without executing their bodies.
Known call and return mismatches are rejected before execution. Unannotated positions remain dynamic for source compatibility and keep a runtime guard when they cross a typed boundary.
items.example:
func add1(value u32) u32 => value + u32(1)
emit add1(u32(41)) # 42u32

items.name: macro
items.summary: Define a compile-time `macro`.
details: Macros expand before normal execution and are guarded by an expansion budget.
This keeps accidental infinite expansion from hanging the compiler and tooling.

items.name: emit
items.summary: Append a value to the program output stream.
details: `emit` is valid at the top level and inside synchronously executed blocks, loops, functions, selected call-shaped `if` branches, `match`/`switch` arms, `try`/`catch` bodies, and expanded macro blocks.
It evaluates once, commits one ordered output value, and continues. Earlier output remains visible after a later error or cancellation.
Module initialization and concurrent `spawn`, `parallel`, `race`, `select`, or `timeout` bodies cannot emit. Return a value and emit it from the synchronous caller.

items.name: if
items.summary: Select a branch based on a truthy or falsey condition.
details: Conditional expressions are part of the core language, not a library trick.
The `false` branch is optional.

items.name: while
items.summary: Repeat a block `while` a condition remains `true`.
details: The loop body can carry state forward explicitly through bindings.
Use `while` when the stop condition is naturally predicate-based.
items.example: while i < n { let i = i + 1 }

items.name: for
items.summary: Iterate over a sequence or range with a named loop variable.
details: For loops are best for ordered iteration over ranges, lists, and other sequence-like values.
items.example: for x in range(0, 10) { emit x }

items.name: return
items.summary: Exit a function early and yield a result.
details: `return` is only meaningful inside function bodies.
It keeps recursive and branching code readable.

items.name: break
items.summary: Exit the nearest loop.
details: `break` is used for early loop termination when the stopping condition is data-dependent.

items.name: continue
items.summary: Skip to the next loop iteration.
details: `continue` is useful when the loop body contains filtering or guard logic.

items.name: try/catch
items.summary: Catch runtime failures explicitly.
details: The `catch` binding receives the error value.
This keeps failures visible and local to the source that handles them.
items.example: emit try { uint("not-a-number") } catch err { err }

items.name: match
items.returns: The value of the first matching arm.
items.summary: Evaluate a value once and select an expression by pattern.
details: Patterns may be literals, wildcards, bindings, fixed-length lists, or qualified enum cases. An arm expression runs only after its pattern matches.
Use `_` or `default` for a catch-all arm. `enum` matches without a catch-all are checked for missing cases before execution.
items.errors: A dynamic unmatched value reports an error. Invalid, duplicate, unreachable, or non-exhaustive enum arms are source-located diagnostics.

items.name: switch
items.returns: The value of the first matching arm.
items.summary: Use `match` semantics with `switch`-oriented spelling for a multi-branch expression.
details: `switch` evaluates its subject once and accepts the same patterns, guards, wildcard, and enum-exhaustiveness rules as `match`.
Choose `switch` when its branch-table presentation makes the surrounding code easier to scan; it does not change matching or return semantics.
items.errors: A dynamic unmatched value reports an error. Invalid, duplicate, unreachable, or non-exhaustive enum arms are source-located diagnostics.

groups.title: std/text
groups.summary: Unicode-aware string comparison, search, cutting, splitting, trimming, replacement, and text shaping.

items.name: trim
items.parameters: `value` is one UTF-8 `string`.
items.summary: Remove leading and trailing Unicode whitespace from a string.
details: `trim` is the original spelling of `trim_space`; both recognize Unicode whitespace rather than only ASCII spaces.
An empty string and a string containing only whitespace both produce an empty string.
items.errors: Wrong arity or a non-string argument produces a structured `invalid_argument` or `type_error`.

items.name: upper
items.parameters: `value` is one UTF-8 `string`.
items.summary: Convert Unicode letters in a string to uppercase.
details: Conversion uses Unicode case mappings and is locale-independent.
Non-letter code points and the empty string are preserved.
Native C support is limited to the parity-tested UTF-8 case-mapping slice; unsupported module members still fail during compilation.
items.errors: Wrong arity or a non-string argument produces a structured `invalid_argument` or `type_error`.

items.name: lower
items.parameters: `value` is one UTF-8 `string`.
items.summary: Convert Unicode letters in a string to lowercase.
details: Conversion uses Unicode case mappings and is locale-independent.
Use `equal_fold` for case-insensitive equality; lowercasing is not a general normalization or collation operation.
items.errors: Wrong arity or a non-string argument produces a structured `invalid_argument` or `type_error`.

items.name: fields
items.parameters: `value` is one UTF-8 `string`.
items.summary: Split text around runs of Unicode whitespace.
details: Empty fields are discarded, and Unicode whitespace includes spaces, tabs, and non-ASCII whitespace code points.
The result is a newly owned list of newly owned strings. This member is part of the parity-tested Native C slice.
items.errors: Wrong arity, a non-string argument, malformed UTF-8, or an allocation failure produces a structured error.

items.name: compare
items.parameters: `left` and `right` are UTF-8 strings.
items.summary: Compare two strings lexicographically.
details: The result is exactly `-1`, `0`, or `1`, using UTF-8 byte ordering with code-point boundaries preserved by valid input.
The Native C implementation compares only the common prefix before applying length ordering, so a shorter string is not always smaller.
items.errors: Wrong arity, a non-string argument, or malformed UTF-8 produces a structured error.

items.name: equal_fold
items.parameters: `left` and `right` are UTF-8 strings.
items.summary: Compare strings using Unicode simple case folding.
details: The operation is locale-independent and recognizes the compact portable equivalence table, including final sigma, Kelvin sign, and long s mappings.
It returns a scalar and never retains either input.
items.errors: Wrong arity, a non-string argument, or malformed UTF-8 produces a structured error.

items.name: count
items.parameters: `value` and `needle` are UTF-8 strings.
items.summary: Count non-overlapping occurrences of a substring.
details: Matches advance by the complete needle, so `text.count("aaaa", "aa")` is `2` rather than `3`.
An empty needle counts code-point boundaries plus one.
items.errors: Wrong arity, a non-string argument, or malformed UTF-8 produces a structured error.

items.name: index
items.parameters: `value` and `needle` are UTF-8 strings.
items.summary: Return the first matching code-point index.
details: The index counts Unicode code points rather than UTF-8 bytes. A missing match returns `none`; an empty needle returns `some(0)`.
The option is newly owned and does not expose a pointer into the input string.
items.errors: Wrong arity, a non-string argument, or malformed UTF-8 produces a structured error.

items.name: last_index
items.parameters: `value` and `needle` are UTF-8 strings.
items.summary: Return the final matching code-point index.
details: Matches are searched from the end without overlapping result ownership. A missing match returns `none`; an empty needle returns the text length in code points.
The Native C implementation handles an empty needle before scanning so it never advances past the string terminator.
items.errors: Wrong arity, a non-string argument, or malformed UTF-8 produces a structured error.

items.name: replace
items.parameters: `value`, `old`, and `replacement` are UTF-8 strings.
items.summary: Replace all occurrences of one substring with another.
details: Matches are non-overlapping and replacement proceeds from left to right.
An empty `old` value matches before the first code point and after each code point, including in an empty input.
items.errors: Wrong arity, a non-string argument, or a result too large for the host allocation limit produces a structured error.

items.name: repeat
items.parameters: `value` is a UTF-8 string; `count` is an exact integer-compatible value that fits the host allocation index width and is at least zero.
items.summary: Repeat a `string` a fixed number of times.
details: A zero count or an empty input returns an empty string.
The result remains immutable UTF-8 text. Native C checks the 1 MiB result bound before allocation and returns an owned string.
items.errors: Wrong arity, invalid kinds, a negative count, or a result too large for the host allocation limit produces a structured error.

items.name: split
items.parameters: `value` and `separator` are UTF-8 strings.
items.summary: Split text into parts around a delimiter.
details: Every non-overlapping separator is removed and the surrounding substrings are returned; adjacent or trailing separators therefore produce empty elements.
An empty separator splits after each Unicode code point. Splitting an empty string on an empty separator returns an empty list.
items.errors: Wrong arity or a non-string argument produces a structured `invalid_argument` or `type_error`.

items.name: join
items.parameters: `separator` is a UTF-8 string and `parts` is a list. Each list value is rendered with the ordinary text conversion.
items.summary: Join a list of rendered values with a separator.
details: The separator appears only between elements; an empty or one-element list adds no separator.
For a non-empty separator, `join(separator, split(value, separator))` reconstructs `value`.
`join` is part of the parity-tested native C `std/text` subset.
items.errors: Wrong arity, a non-string separator, or a non-list second argument produces a structured error.

items.name: chunks
items.parameters: `value` is a UTF-8 string; `size` is a positive exact integer-compatible code-point count that fits the host allocation index width.
items.summary: Break text into fixed-width pieces.
details: Chunk widths count Unicode code points, never UTF-8 bytes. The final chunk may be shorter.
An empty input returns an empty list.
Native C directly lowers this bounded pure operation, copies each chunk into an owned string, and requires no host capability.
items.errors: Wrong arity, invalid kinds, a non-positive size, or an out-of-range size produces a structured error.

items.name: slug
items.parameters: `value` is one UTF-8 `string`.
items.summary: Turn text into a predictable slug form.
details: Unicode letters and digits are lowercased and preserved. Each run of other code points becomes one ASCII hyphen, with leading and trailing hyphens removed.
An input without letters or digits produces an empty string.
`slug` is part of the parity-tested native C `std/text` subset.
items.errors: Wrong arity or a non-string argument produces a structured `invalid_argument` or `type_error`.

items.name: cat
items.parameters: Zero or more values of any runtime kind accepted by ordinary text rendering.
items.summary: Concatenate values as text.
details: Values are rendered in source order without a separator.
With no values, `cat()` returns an empty string.
items.errors: The function itself accepts every arity; an unrenderable future runtime kind would produce a structured error.

groups.title: std/math
groups.summary: Exact arithmetic, numeric constructors, transcendental functions, tensors, and linear algebra.

items.name: iN
items.summary: Construct an explicit signed fixed-width integer.
details: Osiris keeps the width explicit so the compiler, encoder, and runtime can preserve it through analysis and native lowering.

items.name: uN
items.summary: Construct an explicit unsigned fixed-width integer.
details: This family includes `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `u128`, `u256`, `u512`, `u1024`; `uint` is the `u64` constructor and `byte` is the `u8` constructor.
Osiris keeps the width explicit so the compiler, encoder, and runtime can preserve it through analysis and native lowering.

items.name: ufN
items.summary: Construct a packed unsigned numeric form for dense layouts.
details: This family includes `uf8`, `uf16`, `uf32`, `ufnum`, `uf64`, `uf128`, `uf256`, `uf512`, `uf1024`.
Osiris keeps the width explicit so the compiler, encoder, and runtime can preserve it through analysis and native lowering.

items.name: bfN
items.summary: Construct a low-precision or bfloat-style floating-point value.
details: This family includes `bf8`, `bf16`, `bf32`, `bf64`, `bf128`, `bf256`, `bf512`, `bf1024`.
Osiris keeps the width explicit so the compiler, encoder, and runtime can preserve it through analysis and native lowering.

items.name: f32
items.summary: Construct a 32-bit explicit float.
details: `f32` accepts exactly one numeric value and returns that value rounded to the language's explicit 32-bit floating representation. Non-numeric input is an error.

`number` remains the default literal type, but explicit float widths are useful when precision choice matters. Use `f32` when you want hardware-friendly single-precision semantics and visible `f32` output/inference.

Native C lowers a proven scalar floating input directly with one C `float` conversion. Integer, `decimal`, `complex`, `tensor`, and other value families retain their representation-aware native paths.

items.name: f64
items.summary: Construct a 64-bit explicit float.
details: `f64` accepts exactly one numeric value and returns that value in the language's explicit 64-bit floating representation. Non-numeric input is an error.

`number` remains the default literal type, but explicit float widths are useful when precision choice matters. Use `f64` when you want the familiar double-precision path and visible `f64` output/inference.

Native C lowers a proven scalar floating input directly with one C `double` conversion. Integer, `decimal`, `complex`, `tensor`, and other value families retain their representation-aware native paths.

items.name: decimal
items.summary: Construct an exact `decimal` value.
details: Use this for `decimal` math that should stay exact instead of collapsing into approximate float math.

items.name: rat
items.summary: Construct an exact `rational` value.
details: Use this as the alias-shaped `rational` constructor when fraction form matters.

items.name: rational
items.summary: Construct an exact `rational` value.
details: This is the explicit `rational` constructor for fraction-preserving math.
It keeps arithmetic exact where possible instead of collapsing into approximate float math.

items.name: bigint
items.summary: Construct an exact integer value with unbounded width.
details: Useful for combinatorics, cryptography, and large exact powers.

items.name: bigfloat
items.summary: Construct a high-precision floating-point value.
details: Useful when `float64` is not enough and exact or controlled precision matters.

items.name: interval
items.summary: Construct an `interval` with exact lower and upper bounds.
details: Useful for bounded numeric reasoning and conservative error tracking.

items.name: fixed
items.summary: Construct a signed `fixed`-point number.
details: Good for DSP, finance, and deterministic numeric pipelines.

items.name: modint
items.summary: Construct an integer in modular arithmetic.
details: Useful for number theory, hashing, and finite-field style work.

items.name: complex
items.summary: Construct a `complex` value from one `complex`-compatible value or separate real and imaginary components.
details: A pair of `f32` components produces `complex<f32>`; `f64` components produce `complex<f64>`. A default numeric component mixed with `f32` widens to `complex<f64>`, so precision is never silently narrowed.
The `i` suffix creates an imaginary literal and preserves an `f32` or `f64` suffix: `1.25f32i` and `1.25f64i`. Width survives VM execution, inference, text rendering, and codec round trips.

The native C `ABI` currently lowers the default/`f64` `complex` family. A `complex<f32>` literal is rejected at compile time until its dedicated native `ABI` is implemented; it is never widened silently.

items.name: dual
items.summary: Construct a scalar first-order `dual` number for automatic differentiation.
details: `primal` is the ordinary value and `tangent` is its derivative with respect to the chosen seed. Ordinary numeric operands are promoted to `dual(value, 0)` at an arithmetic boundary.
The initial scalar contract supports unary negation, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, equality, `primal`, and `tangent`. Tensor lifting and transcendental derivative rules are intentionally not implemented yet.
`run` and `vm` preserve the `dual` value; `encode`/`decode` preserves both IEEE-754 components. Native C compilation rejects `dual` calls until a dedicated tagged `ABI` exists.

items.name: poly
items.summary: Construct a normalized polynomial from coefficients in ascending degree order.
details: `T` is `number`, `f32`, or `f64`. Trailing zero coefficients are removed while the zero polynomial retains one zero coefficient.
Polynomial values preserve coefficient width and support `+`, `-`, `*`, indexing, `poly_degree`, and `poly_eval`.
items.example:
let p = poly<number>([1, 2, 3])
emit p # poly<number>(1, 2, 3)

items.name: poly_degree
items.summary: Return the normalized degree of a polynomial.
details: The zero polynomial has degree zero. The operation rejects non-polynomial values.

items.name: poly_eval
items.summary: Evaluate a polynomial using deterministic Horner arithmetic.
details: The evaluation value is converted to the polynomial coefficient family; incompatible widths and non-numeric values fail.

items.name: quat
items.summary: Construct a four-component quaternion.
details: Components use `w, x, y, z` order and retain `number`, `f32`, or `f64` width. Quaternion multiplication uses the Hamilton convention.

items.name: quat_conjugate
items.summary: Negate the vector components of a quaternion.
details: The scalar component is retained and the coefficient family is unchanged.

items.name: quat_norm
items.summary: Return the Euclidean norm of a quaternion.
details: The result retains the quaternion coefficient family. Invalid values are rejected with a structured diagnostic.

items.name: quat_inverse
items.summary: Return the multiplicative inverse of a nonzero quaternion.
details: A zero quaternion fails deterministically instead of producing a non-finite result.

items.name: simd
items.summary: Construct a fixed-width SIMD value with numeric or boolean lanes.
details: Lane counts are powers of two from 2 through 16. Numeric lanes support elementwise arithmetic; boolean lanes are used as masks.

items.name: simd_mask
items.summary: Construct a boolean SIMD mask from truthy lane values.
details: The lane count is inferred from the bounded input collection and must satisfy the SIMD lane contract.

items.name: simd_select
items.summary: Select corresponding lanes using a boolean SIMD mask.
details: The mask and both values must have matching lane counts and element families.
items.example: emit simd_select(simd_mask([true, false]), simd<2, number>(2, [1, 2]), simd<2, number>(2, [3, 4]))

items.name: sparse_matrix
items.summary: Construct a canonical two-dimensional sparse matrix.
details: Entries are coordinate/value rows. Duplicate coordinates are summed, zero entries are removed, and coordinates are sorted lexicographically. `format` is `csr` or `csc`.

items.name: sparse_tensor
items.summary: Construct a canonical n-dimensional COO sparse tensor.
details: Coordinates are bounds-checked, duplicate values are summed, zero entries are removed, and iteration is lexicographically deterministic.

items.name: nnz
items.summary: Return the number of stored nonzero entries in a sparse value.
details: The count reflects canonical zero elision and duplicate aggregation.

items.name: to_dense
items.summary: Expand a sparse matrix or tensor into a dense tensor.
details: Missing coordinates use the exact zero of the stored element family. Shape and width metadata are retained.

items.name: to_sparse
items.summary: Convert a dense tensor to its canonical sparse representation.
details: Rank two tensors become sparse matrices; other ranks become sparse tensors. Zero values are omitted and the optional format is validated.

items.name: primal
items.summary: Project the ordinary value from a `dual` number.
details: For `dual(primal, tangent)`, `primal` returns the first component. A non-`dual` input is returned unchanged, so generic code can inspect an AD result without a separate branch.

items.name: tangent
items.summary: Project the first-order derivative from a `dual` number.
details: For `dual(primal, tangent)`, `tangent` returns the derivative seed. A real numeric input has zero tangent. Non-numeric values are rejected.

items.name: real
items.summary: Read the `real` component of a `complex`-compatible value.
details: For `complex<f32>` and `complex<f64>`, `real` preserves the same component width and returns `f32` or `f64`. A default `complex` returns the default `number` family.
A real scalar is accepted only when it is `complex`-compatible; a `complex` with a nonzero imaginary part cannot be coerced by an ordinary numeric cast.

For a real floating scalar, `real` returns that scalar unchanged. Native C lowers this scalar `f32`/`f64`/default-float case directly; `complex`, `tensor`, integer, and other value families retain their respective native contracts.

items.name: imag
items.summary: Read the imaginary component of a `complex`-compatible value.
details: For `complex<f32>` and `complex<f64>`, `imag` preserves the component width. This makes it safe to split a typed `complex` value and reconstruct it without an implicit widening step.
For a real-compatible input, `imag` returns zero in that input's scalar family.
Native C lowers real floating scalar inputs directly to a same-width zero. Complex and aggregate projections retain their separate native representation contracts.

items.name: conjugate
items.returns: same scalar, `complex`, or `tensor` family as value
items.summary: Return the `complex` `conjugate` while preserving real values.
details: For a `complex` scalar `a + bi`, `conjugate` returns `a - bi` and preserves the `complex` component width. Applying `conjugate` twice returns the original value.
Real numeric values are returned unchanged. For tensors, `conjugate` is applied element-wise and the `tensor` shape is retained.
Native C lowers a proven real floating or fixed-width integer scalar as an identity assignment. `complex` and `tensor` conjugation use their owned native value paths.

items.name: magnitude
items.summary: Read the `magnitude` of a `complex` value.
details: For a `complex` value `a + bi`, `magnitude` is `sqrt(a² + b²)`, returned in the promoted floating component family. It is the radial length of the complex-plane representation.

For a real floating scalar, `magnitude` is its absolute value and preserves `f32`, `f64`, or default-float style. Unsigned integers are already non-negative, so `magnitude` returns the same width and value. Signed integers, `decimal`, `quantity`, `bigint`, and `complex` values follow their own representation-preserving `magnitude` rules.

Native C lowers a proven real floating scalar through width-aware absolute value, a proven unsigned scalar as an identity, and proven `i8`/`i16`/`i32` values with width-aware bit arithmetic. `complex`, `i64`, and other value families use their separate native contracts.

items.name: abs
items.summary: Return the absolute value of a number.
details: For floating values, `abs` returns a same-width non-negative floating result. For unsigned values it returns the input unchanged, preserving its declared width and packed/native style.
Signed integers, `bigint`, `decimal`, `quantity`, and `complex` values retain their own representation-aware absolute-value rules; use `magnitude` when you specifically want complex-plane length.

Native C lowers proven floating scalars through width-aware absolute value, unsigned scalars as identity assignments, and `i8`/`i16`/`i32` scalars with width-aware bit arithmetic. `i64` remains on its separate native path.

items.name: min
items.summary: Choose the smaller of two values.
details: Useful anywhere you need a lower bound selection.

items.name: max
items.summary: Choose the larger of two values.
details: Useful anywhere you need an upper bound selection.

items.name: clamp
items.summary: Constrain a value to a closed range.
details: This is the common bounded numeric primitive.

items.name: floor
items.summary: Round down toward negative infinity.
details: Use this for binning and lower-bound discretization.

items.name: ceil
items.summary: Round up toward positive infinity.
details: Use this for upper-bound discretization and allocation math.

items.name: round
items.summary: Round to the nearest integer-like value.
details: Useful for formatting, discretization, and centered rounding.

items.name: sign
items.summary: Return the sign of a value.
details: This yields a directional scalar useful in piecewise math.

items.name: step
items.summary: Return a step-function style threshold value.
details: Useful in control flow and activation-style transforms.

items.name: heaviside
items.summary: Return the Heaviside threshold value.
details: This is a conventional piecewise helper in scientific code.

items.name: relu
items.summary: Apply a rectified-linear transform.
details: This is useful in machine-learning-style numeric code.

items.name: sigmoid
items.summary: Apply a sigmoid transform.
details: Useful for smooth activations and bounded probabilistic transforms.

items.name: softplus
items.summary: Apply a softplus transform.
details: This is a smooth, positive activation-style transform.

items.name: sin
items.parameters: `x` is a real numeric scalar or complex scalar.
items.summary: Compute the real or complex sine.
details: Real inputs retain their floating width. Complex inputs use the principal analytic sine and retain component width.
Complex native-C lowering is deliberately rejected until its special-value and branch behavior has executable parity.

items.name: cos
items.parameters: `x` is a real numeric scalar or complex scalar.
items.summary: Compute the real or complex cosine.
details: Real inputs retain their floating width. Complex inputs use the principal analytic cosine and retain component width.
Complex native-C lowering is deliberately rejected until its special-value behavior has executable parity.

items.name: tan
items.parameters: `x` is a real numeric scalar or complex scalar.
items.summary: Compute the real or complex tangent.
details: Real inputs retain their floating width. Complex inputs use the principal analytic tangent and retain component width.
Poles and IEEE special values follow the shared complex implementation; complex native-C lowering is unsupported.

items.name: asin
items.summary: Compute the inverse sine.
details: Useful for geometry and angle reconstruction.

items.name: acos
items.summary: Compute the inverse cosine.
details: Useful for geometry and angle reconstruction.

items.name: atan
items.summary: Compute the inverse tangent.
details: Useful for geometry, coordinate transforms, and signal work.

items.name: sinh
items.parameters: `x` is a real numeric scalar, complex scalar, or a list/tensor recursively containing supported values.
items.returns: matching scalar, list, or tensor shape
items.summary: Compute the real or complex hyperbolic sine.
details: Scalar results retain real floating style or complex component width; lists and tensors are mapped recursively without changing shape.
Complex native-C lowering is unsupported.

items.name: cosh
items.parameters: `x` is a real numeric scalar, complex scalar, or a list/tensor recursively containing supported values.
items.returns: matching scalar, list, or tensor shape
items.summary: Compute the real or complex hyperbolic cosine.
details: Scalar results retain real floating style or complex component width; lists and tensors are mapped recursively without changing shape.
Complex native-C lowering is unsupported.

items.name: tanh
items.parameters: `x` is a real numeric scalar, complex scalar, or a list/tensor recursively containing supported values.
items.returns: matching scalar, list, or tensor shape
items.summary: Compute the real or complex hyperbolic tangent.
details: Scalar results retain real floating style or complex component width; lists and tensors are mapped recursively without changing shape.
Complex native-C lowering is unsupported.

items.name: asinh
items.summary: Compute the inverse hyperbolic sine.
details: This completes the hyperbolic math family.

items.name: acosh
items.summary: Compute the inverse hyperbolic cosine.
details: This completes the hyperbolic math family.

items.name: atanh
items.summary: Compute the inverse hyperbolic tangent.
details: This completes the hyperbolic math family.

items.name: exp
items.parameters: `x` is a real floating-compatible scalar or a complex scalar.
items.summary: Compute the natural exponential for a real or complex scalar.
details: Real inputs retain the existing floating-width behavior and reject an infinite or NaN result as overflow.
Complex inputs use the principal complex exponential, retain their component width, and follow deterministic IEEE special-value behavior. Complex native-C lowering is deliberately unsupported.

items.name: expm1
items.summary: Compute `exp(x) - 1` with better precision near zero.
details: This keeps small-value precision intact.

items.name: pow
items.parameters: `x` and `y` are exact integers, real numeric scalars, or complex scalars. A complex call may mix complex and floating operands.
items.returns: exact integer, floating-point, or complex scalar
items.summary: Raise a value to a power.
details: `pow` first attempts exact integer exponentiation when both operands can be interpreted as integers and the exponent is non-negative. That branch preserves integer style and may produce a `bigint` rather than a floating value.

When exact exponentiation does not apply, `pow` uses floating power semantics and returns a floating numeric scalar. Fully `f32` floating inputs narrow once to `f32`; `f64` or default floating inputs retain their corresponding floating result style.
A negative or fractional exponent bypasses the exact branch. Floating exceptional values follow the underlying IEEE numeric result instead of introducing a separate Osiris domain error.
When either operand is complex, `pow` uses principal complex logarithm/exponential semantics, retains the promoted component width, and bypasses exact-integer exponentiation.

Native C lowering currently admits only statically known `f32` literal operands for which the exact-integer branch is proven inapplicable. Exact, `f64`, mixed-width, dynamic, and unproven calls are rejected at native compile time so a C `pow` call cannot silently change the language result kind.

items.name: expt
items.parameters: `x` and `y` accept the same exact-integer, real, and complex families as `pow`.
items.returns: exact integer, floating-point, or complex scalar
items.summary: Alias-shaped power helper for exact integer style code.
details: `expt` has exactly the same behavior, result type, and errors as `pow`; it is an alternate spelling for users who prefer exact-math terminology.

Integer-like operands with a non-negative exponent first use exact exponentiation and preserve integer style, potentially returning a `bigint`. Other real numeric inputs use floating power semantics; a complex operand selects the same principal complex operation as `pow`.

Native C lowering has the same narrow contract as `pow`: only statically known non-exact `f32` literal calls lower directly. Exact, `f64`, mixed-width, dynamic, and unproven calls reject at native compile time rather than losing the exact result-kind rule.

items.name: log
items.parameters: `x` and optional `base` are real floating-compatible or complex scalars. A complex call may mix complex and floating operands.
items.summary: Compute the natural logarithm, or a logarithm in an explicit base.
details: With one argument, `log(x)` is the natural logarithm. With a base, `log(x, base)` is evaluated as `log(x) / log(base)`.
Both forms require `x > 0`. The base form additionally requires `base > 0` and `base != 1`; violations raise the `log` domain error.

The result is a floating numeric scalar. An `f32` input produces `f32` after the language's explicit narrowing boundary; `f64` and default floating inputs retain their corresponding floating representation.
When either operand is complex, `log` uses the principal branch with phase in `[-Pi, Pi]`; complex zero is the logarithmic pole. A complex base must not be zero or one.

Native C lowering supports the one-argument floating form. The two-argument form lowers only when both operands are statically proven `f32`; `f64`, mixed-width, and unproven base-`log` calls are rejected at native compile time to preserve exact interpreter parity across Go and C math libraries.

items.name: log10
items.summary: Compute the base-10 logarithm.
details: Useful when decimal decades are the meaningful scale.

items.name: log2
items.summary: Compute the base-2 logarithm.
details: Useful for binary scale, bit-width reasoning, and powers-of-two analysis.

items.name: log1p
items.summary: Compute `log(1 + x)` with better precision near zero.
details: This is the precision-friendly logarithm variant.

items.name: sqrt
items.parameters: `x` is a real numeric scalar or a complex scalar.
items.summary: Compute the real square root or principal complex square root.
details: Real negative inputs retain the existing domain error. Non-negative real inputs preserve their floating style.

Complex inputs use the principal branch with a non-negative real component; on the negative-real cut, the result's imaginary sign follows the input imaginary zero. Complex native-C lowering is unsupported.

items.name: cbrt
items.summary: Compute the cube root.
details: Useful for geometric and scaling transforms.

items.name: hypot
items.summary: Compute the Euclidean length of a 2D vector.
details: This avoids manual overflow-prone squaring patterns.

items.name: norm
items.summary: Compute a magnitude-style norm.
details: Useful for `vector` and `tensor`-style magnitude checks.

items.name: erf
items.summary: Compute the error function.
details: The error function `erf(x)` is the normalized integral of a Gaussian curve from `0` to `x`.
In standard form, `erf(x) = 2 / sqrt(pi) * integral from 0 to x of e^(-t^2) dt`.
It appears in probability theory, diffusion models, heat flow, statistics, and Gaussian tail calculations.

items.name: erfc
items.summary: Compute the complementary error function.
details: The complementary error function `erfc(x)` is defined as `1 - erf(x)`.
It is written as `erfc(x) = 2 / sqrt(pi) * integral from x to infinity of e^(-t^2) dt`.
It is useful when a problem is expressed in terms of the tail area of a Gaussian distribution instead of the central mass.

items.name: gamma
items.summary: Compute the `gamma` function.
details: The `gamma` function extends the factorial to non-integer values.
For positive integers `n`, `gamma(n) = (n - 1)!`; for half-integers it connects to square roots of pi.
It returns a floating numeric scalar, preserving `f32` or `f64` style when that is the input style; other numeric scalar inputs are converted through the normal floating result rule.

It is used throughout combinatorics, analytic continuation, statistical distributions, and special-function identities. The function follows IEEE numeric behavior for exceptional inputs rather than defining a separate Osiris domain error.

Native C lowering supports a statically proven `f32` scalar input, computed in double precision and narrowed once to `f32`. `f64` and unproven inputs are rejected by the native compiler because Go's and a platform C library's `gamma` implementations do not have a bit-exact shared contract.

items.name: lgamma
items.summary: Compute the logarithm of the `gamma` function.
details: `lgamma(x)` returns the natural logarithm of the gamma function, which is often easier to compute safely than `gamma(x)` itself.
It returns a floating numeric scalar, preserving `f32` or `f64` style when that is the input style; other numeric scalar inputs are converted through the normal floating result rule.

It is especially useful when `gamma(x)` would overflow or when a formula needs stable log-domain arithmetic. Statistics, probability, and asymptotic analysis often use `lgamma` to keep large products numerically manageable.

Native C lowering supports a statically proven `f32` scalar input, computed in double precision and narrowed once to `f32`. `f64` and unproven inputs are rejected by the native compiler because Go's and a platform C library's log-gamma implementations do not have a bit-exact shared contract.

groups.title: Sequences and Ranges
groups.summary: Convenience functions for building dense numeric structures and simple sequences.

items.name: zeros
items.summary: Construct an array filled with zeros.
details: `zeros` creates a dense `tensor` whose entire storage is initialized to 0.
It is the standard starting point for `matrix` assembly, grid initialization, and buffer preparation before a computation writes real values into place.

items.name: ones
items.summary: Construct an array filled with ones.
details: `ones` creates a dense `tensor` whose storage is initialized to 1.
It is commonly used when a multiplicative identity-like shape is needed for normalization, accumulation, or initialization of gain factors.

items.name: full
items.summary: Construct an array filled with a chosen value.
details: `full` creates a dense `tensor` whose entries are all set to the provided value.
This is useful when the computation needs a sentinel value, a constant field, or a prefilled buffer that will later be refined in place.

items.name: eye
items.summary: Construct a square identity `matrix`.
details: `eye` constructs a square `matrix` with ones on the main diagonal and zeros everywhere else.
This is the canonical identity `matrix` and is used in `matrix` algebra, solver setup, and as a neutral element for `matrix` multiplication.

items.name: identity
items.summary: Construct a square identity `matrix`.
details: `identity` is the alias-shaped form of `eye` and produces the same square identity `matrix`.
It exists so the language can read naturally in code that prefers `identity` over the shorter `eye` spelling.

items.name: arange
items.summary: Generate a numeric range with an explicit step.
details: `arange` generates a sequence that advances from `start` toward `stop` using a fixed `step` size.
It is the regular numeric ramp constructor and is useful for sampled grids, iteration tables, and synthetic axis data.

items.name: linspace
items.summary: Generate evenly spaced samples over an interval.
details: `linspace` returns a fixed number of values that divide the interval between `start` and `stop` into equal segments.
It is the usual choice when you care about sample count, endpoint coverage, and predictable spacing rather than a literal step size.

items.name: logspace
items.summary: Generate samples spaced on a logarithmic scale.
details: `logspace` returns samples whose exponents are evenly spaced, then raises the chosen `base` to those exponents.
It is useful for frequency sweeps, order-of-magnitude searches, and any workflow where logarithmic spacing is more meaningful than linear spacing.

items.name: vector
items.summary: Construct a one-dimensional `tensor` from values.
details: `vector` turns a variadic `list` of values into a one-dimensional dense `tensor`.
It is the explicit, readable form of a small numeric `vector` and is useful when the data is naturally flat.

items.name: vec
items.summary: Construct a one-dimensional `tensor` from values.
details: `vec` is the compact spelling of `vector` and produces the same one-dimensional dense `tensor`.
It is useful when the code wants a short, visually light constructor for small numeric sequences.

groups.title: Tensor Computing
groups.summary: Shape-aware dense numeric work with broadcast semantics, views, and linear algebra helpers.

items.name: tensor
items.summary: Construct a dense `tensor` with explicit shape metadata.
details: `tensor` is the core dense numeric container in Osiris and carries shape metadata alongside its flat storage.
The runtime, optimizer, and native lowering passes all treat shape as a first-class property so `tensor` code can be analyzed and specialized instead of handled as generic lists.

items.name: matrix
items.summary: Construct a dense `matrix` with explicit shape metadata.
details: `matrix` is the two-dimensional specialization of `tensor` and is intended for row-column linear algebra work.
It preserves the same shape metadata and lowering benefits as `tensor`, but reads more naturally when the data is explicitly a `matrix`.

items.name: shape
items.summary: Inspect the `shape` of a shape-aware value.
details: `shape` returns the rank and dimension sizes for a `tensor`-like value.
It is the inspection primitive that makes it easy to reason about broadcasting, `reshape` safety, and `matrix` dimensions.

items.name: flatten
items.summary: Flatten a shape-aware value into a linear sequence.
details: `flatten` discards the shape structure and returns the underlying values in linear order.
It is useful when a `tensor` needs to be serialized, inspected, or passed into a routine that expects a flat sequence.

items.name: squeeze
items.summary: Remove singleton dimensions from a `tensor`.
details: `squeeze` removes dimensions whose extent is 1.
It is useful after broadcasting or batch construction when the code wants to recover a simpler shape without changing the underlying values.

items.name: expand_dims
items.summary: Add a singleton dimension to a `tensor`.
details: `expand_dims` inserts a new axis of size 1 at the requested position.
It is the opposite of `squeeze` and is commonly used to make a value broadcast-compatible or to make a batch axis explicit.

items.name: concat
items.summary: Combine tensors along an axis.
details: `concat` joins compatible tensors along a shared axis so their data becomes one larger `tensor`.
It is useful for assembling batches, extending datasets, and combining chunks of `tensor` work without flattening them first.

items.name: stack
items.summary: Stack tensors by adding a new dimension.
details: `stack` joins tensors by creating a new axis rather than reusing an existing one.
It is the direct way to build a batch dimension or any other higher-rank structure from a collection of equal-shaped inputs.

items.name: broadcast_to
items.summary: Broadcast a value to a requested shape.
details: `broadcast_to` expands a value across a larger shape according to broadcasting rules.
It is useful when a scalar or smaller `tensor` must participate in elementwise work alongside a larger shape.

items.name: where
items.summary: Select values conditionally across shapes.
details: `where` chooses between two values elementwise based on a boolean condition.
It is the vectorized branch operator for `tensor` math and is the array-native equivalent of an `if` expression.

items.name: clip
items.summary: Clamp values to a lower and upper bound.
details: `clip` constrains each value into the closed interval between `lo` and `hi`.
It is useful for bounded activations, normalization, range safety, and any numeric pipeline that should not escape a fixed interval.

items.name: gather
items.summary: Gather elements by index.
details: `gather` builds a new `tensor` by selecting entries from the source at the provided indexes.
It is the read-side companion to `scatter` and is common in lookup, sampling, and embedding-style workflows.

items.name: scatter
items.summary: Scatter elements into a base `tensor` by index.
details: `scatter` writes values into a base `tensor` at the provided positions.
It is the write-side companion to `gather` and is common in indexed updates, sparse placement, and reconstruction workflows.

items.name: pad
items.summary: Pad `tensor` data to a larger shape.
details: `pad` extends a `tensor` with additional boundary elements according to the selected padding policy.
It is used when windows, borders, or fixed-size kernels need data to exist past the original edge.

items.name: tile
items.summary: Repeat `tensor` data across dimensions.
details: `tile` repeats `tensor` data across one or more axes to form a larger repeated structure.
It is useful for patterned expansion, grid construction, and repeated layout generation.

items.name: transpose
items.summary: Transpose a `tensor` or `matrix`.
details: `transpose` swaps axes in a `tensor` and is the canonical row-column transform for matrices.
It is a core dense layout operation and often changes how data is traversed in later linear algebra steps.

items.name: dot
items.summary: Compute a `dot` product.
details: `dot` computes the sum of pairwise products across matching elements.
It is the scalar-product primitive behind projections, similarity measures, and the inner loops of `matrix` multiplication.

items.name: matmul
items.summary: Compute `matrix` multiplication.
details: `matmul` performs dense `matrix` multiplication with shape-aware semantics.
It is the central dense linear algebra primitive for transforms, solver setup, and high-throughput numeric code.

items.name: reshape
items.summary: Reinterpret a `tensor` with a new shape when the data layout allows it.
details: `reshape` keeps the underlying values but changes the shape metadata used to interpret them.
It is the preferred way to present the same contiguous storage under a different view when the element count still matches.

items.name: outer
items.summary: Construct an `outer` product.
details: `outer` forms a `matrix` or higher-rank `tensor` from every pairwise combination of the inputs.
It is useful for basis construction, `tensor` products, and diagnostics that need the full pairwise interaction table.

items.name: trace
items.summary: Read the diagonal `trace` of a `matrix`.
details: `trace` sums the entries on the main diagonal of a `matrix`; rectangular matrices use their shorter dimension.
It is a standard diagnostic in linear algebra and is often used in invariants, projections, and `matrix` summaries.

items.name: det
items.summary: Compute a `matrix` determinant.
details: `det` returns the determinant, which encodes scale factor and invertibility information for a square `matrix`.
It is a classic dense linear algebra workhorse and is used in solving systems, geometry, and change-of-basis reasoning.

items.name: solve
items.summary: Solve a linear system.
details: `solve` computes the `vector` or `tensor` `x` such that `matrix * x = rhs` when the system is solvable.
It is the direct linear-system primitive used in fitting, calibration, physics, and numerical analysis.

items.name: inv
items.summary: Invert a `matrix`.
details: `inv` computes the multiplicative inverse of a square `matrix` when one exists.
It is often used in algebraic derivations, solver formulations, and analytic `matrix` transforms, although `solve` is usually preferred numerically.

items.name: qr
items.summary: Compute a QR factorization.
details: `qr` factors a `matrix` into orthogonal and triangular components.
It is useful in least-squares solving, orthonormal basis construction, and numerically stable decomposition-based workflows.

items.name: cholesky
items.summary: Compute a Cholesky factorization.
details: `cholesky` computes the lower-triangular factor from the `matrix`'s lower triangle and requires every diagonal pivot to stay positive.
It is a preferred decomposition for covariance systems, optimization, and fast structured solves.

items.name: eig
items.summary: Compute an eigenvalue decomposition.
details: `eig` computes the eigenstructure of a `matrix`, returning values that describe how the `matrix` scales its eigenvectors.
It is central to stability analysis, modal decomposition, dynamical systems, and spectral reasoning.

items.name: eigh
items.summary: Compute an eigenvalue decomposition for symmetric matrices.
details: `eigh` is the symmetric or Hermitian-specialized eigen decomposition path.
It is typically preferred when the input is known to be symmetric because that structure allows more stable and efficient computation.

items.name: svd
items.summary: Compute a singular value decomposition.
details: `svd` decomposes a `matrix` into orthogonal factors and singular values that measure the strength of its principal directions.
It is one of the most useful numerical linear algebra tools for compression, rank analysis, pseudoinverses, and stable approximation.

groups.title: Reductions and statistics
groups.summary: Summaries, aggregations, and elementwise collection-wide numeric helpers.

items.name: mean
items.summary: Compute the average.
details: `mean` adds the elements of a collection and divides by their count.
It is the ordinary center-of-mass style summary used in almost every descriptive numeric workflow.

items.name: var
items.summary: Compute the variance.
details: `var` measures how far a collection spreads away from its mean.
It is a primary dispersion statistic and is used throughout uncertainty estimates, modeling, and normalization.

items.name: std
items.summary: Compute the standard deviation.
details: `std` is the square root of variance and expresses spread in the original units of the data.
It is often easier to interpret than variance and is one of the most common statistics in analysis and reporting.

items.name: median
items.summary: Compute the median.
details: `median` returns the middle value after the data is ordered, or the midpoint between the two middle values for an even-sized collection.
It is more robust than the mean when the data has outliers or long tails.

items.name: quantile
items.summary: Compute a quantile.
details: `quantile` returns the value below which a chosen fraction of the data falls.
It is the general form of percentile-based analysis and is useful for distribution thresholds and robust summaries.

items.name: percentile
items.summary: Compute a percentile.
details: `percentile` is the human-friendly quantile form expressed as a percentage from 0 to 100.
It is useful for summarizing ranks, thresholds, and distribution tails in reports and analysis pipelines.

items.name: argmin
items.summary: Return the position of the smallest element.
details: `argmin` scans the collection and returns the index of the smallest observed value.
It is useful whenever you need the location of an extreme rather than the extreme's numeric value.

items.name: argmax
items.summary: Return the position of the largest element.
details: `argmax` scans the collection and returns the index of the largest observed value.
It is useful whenever you need the location of an extreme rather than the extreme's numeric value.

items.name: any
items.summary: Collapse a boolean collection to a single truth value.
details: `any` returns `true` when at least one value in the collection is `true`.
It is the standard existential reduction and is useful for validation, filtering, and guard conditions.

items.name: all
items.summary: Collapse a boolean collection to a single truth value.
details: `all` returns `true` only when every value in the collection is `true`.
It is the standard universal reduction and is useful for validation, invariants, and guard conditions.

items.name: cumsum
items.summary: Return cumulative sums.
details: `cumsum` returns the running prefix sum of a collection.
It is useful for cumulative totals, histogram-like accumulation, and any workflow that needs the trajectory of partial sums.

items.name: cumprod
items.summary: Return cumulative products.
details: `cumprod` returns the running prefix product of a collection.
It is useful for multiplicative growth, compounded factors, and any workflow that needs the trajectory of partial products.

groups.title: I/O helpers
groups.summary: Explicit file, stream, and structured-input helpers for deterministic data pipelines.

items.name: read
items.summary: Read a file as text.
details: Use this when the file is text and you want a `string` result.

items.name: readbytes
items.summary: Read a file as raw bytes.
details: Use this when the file is binary or when you need exact byte access.

items.name: write
items.summary: Write text or byte-compatible data to a file.
details: The current implementation returns success as a `true` boolean value.

items.name: lines
items.summary: Split text or bytes into line records.
details: This is useful for line-oriented file and stream processing.

items.name: csv
items.summary: Parse CSV data into nested Osiris values.
details: Each row is returned as a `list` of cell values.

items.name: jsonparse
items.summary: Parse JSON into native Osiris values.
details: JSON numbers are preserved with exactness where possible.

items.name: openread
items.summary: Open a file for explicit line or chunk reading.
details: Use `readline` or `readchunk`, then `close` the handle when processing is complete.

items.name: openwrite
items.summary: Open a file for buffered, explicit streaming writes.
details: Use `writechunk`, `flush` when required, and `close` the handle when processing is complete.

items.name: readline
items.summary: Read one line from a readable stream without retaining its line ending.
details: The returned text excludes a trailing `LF` or `CRLF`. At end-of-file it returns `null` rather than an empty text value.
Each call advances the handle, allowing line-oriented processing without loading the entire input.
items.errors: The handle must be open and readable. Wrong arity, a non-stream value, a closed stream, and host I/O failures are errors.

items.name: readchunk
items.summary: Read up to `size` bytes from a readable stream as exact `uint8` values.
details: A zero `size` returns an empty `list`. A short `list` is valid when fewer than `size` bytes are available; `null` means no bytes remain at end-of-file.
Each call advances the handle and bounds the temporary read buffer to the requested `size`.
items.errors: `size` must be a non-negative integer. The handle must be open and readable; wrong arity, a non-stream value, and host I/O failures are errors.

items.name: writechunk
items.summary: Append byte-compatible data to a writable stream's bounded user-space buffer.
details: `data` may be text, a byte `list` or `tensor`, or an integer encoded as bytes. The result is the number of bytes accepted by the stream writer.
`writechunk` does not promise that buffered bytes have reached the operating-system descriptor; call `flush` when that boundary matters.
items.errors: The handle must be open and writable. Non-byte-compatible data, wrong arity, a non-stream value, and host write failures are errors.

items.name: flush
items.summary: Flush buffered stream output to its underlying descriptor.
details: `flush` returns `true` after the writer flushes successfully. It is a no-op that returns `true` for an open readable-only handle.
Flushing does not close the handle and does not promise remote receipt for a TCP stream; it only completes the local writer boundary.
items.errors: The handle must be open. Wrong arity, a non-stream value, a closed stream, and host `flush` failures are errors.
items.example:
let out = openwrite("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/out.txt")
emit writechunk(out, "OSR\n") # 4u64
emit flush(out) # true
emit close(out) # true

items.name: close
items.summary: Flush and release the file or TCP descriptor owned by a stream handle.
details: The first successful `close` returns `true`. A later `close` of the same handle returns `false` without reopening or re-closing it.
The handle remains printable after `close`, but later reads, writes, and flushes fail. `close` flushes a writable buffer before releasing the descriptor.
For user-defined resources, `close` dispatches to a zero-argument method, including a method supplied by a trait or interface implementation. Such methods must be idempotent when used with `defer`.
items.errors: The argument must be a built-in handle or a value with a callable zero-argument `close` method. A host flush or descriptor-close failure is returned as an error.
items.example:
let out = openwrite("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/out.txt")
emit writechunk(out, "OSR\n") # 4u64
emit close(out) # true
emit close(out) # false

items.name: transfer
items.summary: Copy ordered bytes between two open streams through a bounded buffer.
details: `source` must be readable and `destination` writable; they must be distinct. The function borrows both handles, flushes the copied bytes before success, and never closes either one.
`limit` is optional and non-negative. Without it `transfer` continues to end-of-file using bounded memory. It preserves `destination` backpressure and returns only bytes accepted by the destination.
Task/session cancellation, TCP deadlines, `close`, and I/O failures remain structured errors. Networking is interpreter/`vm` host I/O only; native C lowering rejects `transfer`.

items.name: append
items.summary: Append exact byte-compatible data without truncating the file.
items.parameters: `path` is a non-empty NUL-free `string`. `data` is a `string`, byte `list` or tensor, or an exact non-negative value supported by the byte encoder.
details: Returns the exact number of bytes appended.
The destination is created with mode `0644` before umask when absent. Existing content and permissions are preserved. Success does not imply `fsync` durability.
The call owns its temporary descriptor and closes it before returning.
items.errors: Invalid paths or data are `invalid_argument` or `type_error`; missing parents, permissions, storage exhaustion, cancellation, short writes, and close failures use stable structured filesystem kinds.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `append` at its source location.
items.example:
emit write("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/append.txt", "OS") # true
emit append("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/append.txt", "R") # 1u64
emit read("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/append.txt") # "OSR"

items.name: read_limit
items.summary: Read a byte prefix with an explicit allocation ceiling.
items.parameters: `path` is a non-empty NUL-free `string`. `limit` is an exact integer from `0` through `1048576`.
details: Returns at most `limit` exact `uint8` values; reaching the limit is a successful prefix read.
The raw read uses one fixed `32 KiB` work buffer, the returned list is capped at `1048576` width-preserving byte values, and task cancellation is checked between reads.
Use `file_size` when the caller must distinguish a complete file from a prefix.
items.errors: An excessive limit is `resource_exhausted`. Invalid values, missing files, permission failures, cancellation, and host reads use stable structured filesystem kinds.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `read_limit` at its source location.

items.name: copy_file
items.summary: Copy one regular file through a fixed-size buffer.
items.parameters: `source` and `destination` are distinct non-empty NUL-free path strings. The source must resolve to a regular file.
details: Returns the exact number of bytes accepted by the destination.
The destination is created with mode `0644` before umask or truncated if it exists. The copy uses one `32 KiB` buffer and handles short writes.
The operation is not atomic and does not preserve source permissions. On failure, a partial destination can remain.
items.errors: The same resolved source/destination is `invalid_argument`. Path, permission, cancellation, storage, read, write, and close failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `copy_file` at its source location.

items.name: truncate_file
items.summary: Resize a file through an explicit path.
items.parameters: `path` is a non-empty NUL-free `string`. `size` is an exact integer in the signed 64-bit range and must be non-negative.
details: Returns `true` after the hosted truncate succeeds.
Shrinking discards bytes at and after `size`; growing exposes zero bytes under the host filesystem's sparse-file rules.
A final symlink is followed and its target is resized.
items.errors: Invalid sizes, missing paths, permissions, directories, cancellation, and hosted truncate failures use stable structured filesystem kinds.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `truncate_file` at its source location.
items.example:
emit write("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/truncate.txt", "abcdef") # true
