emit truncate_file("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/truncate.txt", 3) # true
emit read("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/truncate.txt") # "abc"

items.name: exists
items.summary: Report whether a path resolves to an existing target.
items.parameters: `path` is a non-empty NUL-free `string`. Final symlinks are followed.
details: Returns `true` for an existing target and `false` for a missing path or broken final symlink.
Permission and other inspection failures remain errors instead of being collapsed into `false`.
items.errors: Invalid paths, permissions, cancellation, and host metadata failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `exists` at its source location.
items.example:
emit exists("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/input.txt") # true
emit exists("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/missing.txt") # false

items.name: file_size
items.summary: Return the byte size of a regular file.
items.parameters: `path` is a non-empty NUL-free `string` resolving to a regular file. Final symlinks are followed.
details: Returns the non-negative hosted file size in bytes.
Directories and non-regular objects are rejected so their platform-specific metadata sizes do not enter the language contract.
items.errors: Missing files, invalid file kinds, permissions, cancellation, and host metadata failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `file_size` at its source location.

items.name: is_file
items.summary: Test whether a path resolves to a regular file.
items.parameters: `path` is a non-empty NUL-free `string`. Final symlinks are followed.
details: Returns `true` only for a regular file and `false` for a directory, missing path, or broken final symlink.
Inspection failures other than absence remain errors.
items.errors: Invalid paths, permissions, cancellation, and host metadata failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `is_file` at its source location.
items.example:
emit is_file("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/input.txt") # true
emit is_file("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__") # false

items.name: is_dir
items.summary: Test whether a path resolves to a directory.
items.parameters: `path` is a non-empty NUL-free `string`. Final symlinks are followed.
details: Returns `true` only for a directory and `false` for a regular file, missing path, or broken final symlink.
Inspection failures other than absence remain errors.
items.errors: Invalid paths, permissions, cancellation, and host metadata failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `is_dir` at its source location.
items.example:
emit is_dir("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__") # true
emit is_dir("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/input.txt") # false

items.name: mkdir
items.summary: Create one directory without creating missing parents.
items.parameters: `path` is a non-empty NUL-free `string`; its parent must already exist.
details: Returns `true` when one directory is created.
The directory uses mode `0755` before umask. An existing path is not treated as success.
items.errors: Existing paths are `already_exists`; a non-directory or missing parent, permissions, cancellation, and host failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `mkdir` at its source location.

items.name: mkdir_all
items.summary: Create a directory path and any missing parent directories.
items.parameters: `path` is a non-empty NUL-free `string`.
details: Returns `true` when the full path is a directory, including when it already existed.
Every new directory uses mode `0755` before umask. This recursive creation does not imply recursive deletion.
items.errors: A non-directory path component, permissions, cancellation, and hosted creation failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `mkdir_all` at its source location.

items.name: read_dir
items.summary: List directory entry names in deterministic lexical order.
items.parameters: `path` names a directory. Optional exact non-negative `limit` defaults to `4096` and cannot exceed `65536`.
details: Returns entry base names as strings sorted in lexical byte order.
A string name is the complete public entry representation; host `FileInfo` and `dirent` metadata are not exposed.
If entry count exceeds the selected limit, the call fails instead of returning an incomplete listing.
items.errors: Excess entries are `resource_exhausted`; non-directories, invalid limits, permissions, cancellation, and hosted reads are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `read_dir` at its source location.
items.example:
emit mkdir_all("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/listing") # true
emit write("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/listing/zeta", "z") # true
emit write("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/listing/alpha", "a") # true
emit read_dir("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/listing") # ["alpha", "zeta"]

items.name: rename
items.summary: Rename one explicit filesystem entry without a copy fallback.
items.parameters: `old_path` and `new_path` are non-empty NUL-free path strings.
details: Returns `true` after the one hosted rename succeeds.
Destination replacement and directory rules remain platform-specific; the API makes no portable atomicity guarantee.
A cross-filesystem rename fails as `io_error` and never becomes copy-and-remove.
items.errors: Missing sources, destination conflicts, permissions, cross-filesystem moves, cancellation, and hosted rename failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `rename` at its source location.
items.example:
emit write("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/before.txt", "data") # true
emit rename("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/before.txt", "__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/after.txt") # true
emit exists("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/after.txt") # true

items.name: remove
items.summary: Remove one explicit file, symlink, or empty directory.
items.parameters: `path` is one non-empty NUL-free path string.
details: Returns `true` after the named entry is removed.
The operation never walks a directory. A final symlink is removed without removing its target.
Use of a non-empty directory fails; this API has no recursive-delete mode.
items.errors: Missing paths, non-empty directories, permissions, cancellation, and hosted removal failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `remove` at its source location.
items.example:
emit write("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/remove.txt", "temporary") # true
emit remove("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/remove.txt") # true
emit exists("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/remove.txt") # false

items.name: openappend
items.summary: Open an owned buffered stream for end-of-file writes.
items.parameters: `path` is a non-empty NUL-free `string`.
details: Returns an owned writable file stream whose initial logical cursor is the current file size.
The file is created with mode `0644` before umask when absent and is never truncated. Hosted append mode places every descriptor write at the then-current end.
The caller must `close` the stream; the first close returns `true` and later closes return `false`.
items.errors: Invalid paths, missing parents, permissions, cancellation, and hosted open failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `openappend` at its source location.
items.example:
emit write("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/stream-append.txt", "OS") # true
let output = openappend("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/stream-append.txt")
emit writechunk(output, "R") # 1u64
emit close(output) # true
emit read("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/stream-append.txt") # "OSR"

items.name: seek
items.summary: Move the logical cursor of an owned file stream.
items.parameters: `stream` is an open file stream, `offset` is an exact signed-64-bit integer, and `origin` is `"start"`, `"current"`, or `"end"`.
details: Returns the new non-negative byte position.
Buffered output is flushed and buffered reader look-ahead is reconciled first. A regular file may seek beyond end-of-file; a negative resulting position is rejected.
TCP and other non-file streams are unsupported.
items.errors: Closed or non-file streams, invalid origins or offsets, cancellation, flush failures, and hosted seek failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `seek` at its source location.
items.example:
let input = openread("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/input.bin")
emit seek(input, -1, "end") # 3u64
emit readchunk(input, 1) # [33u8]
emit close(input) # true

items.name: tell
items.summary: Return a file stream's logical byte position.
items.parameters: `stream` is an open owned file stream.
details: Returns the non-negative logical cursor position.
The result accounts for buffered reader look-ahead and flushes buffered writes before observing their descriptor position.
TCP and other non-file streams are unsupported.
items.errors: Closed or non-file streams, cancellation, flush failures, and hosted cursor failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `tell` at its source location.
items.example:
let input = openread("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/input.bin")
emit readchunk(input, 2) # [79u8, 83u8]
emit tell(input) # 2u64
emit close(input) # true

items.name: truncate
items.summary: Resize the file owned by a writable stream.
items.parameters: `stream` is an open writable file stream. `size` is an exact non-negative integer in the signed 64-bit range.
details: Returns `true` after buffered output is flushed and the file is resized.
The stream cursor is unchanged, including when it lies beyond the new end.
Read-only, TCP, non-file, and closed streams are rejected.
items.errors: Invalid sizes or stream modes, cancellation, flush failures, permissions, and hosted truncate failures are structured.
items.native: Unsupported. Native C compilation rejects `truncate` at its source location.
items.example:
let output = openwrite("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/stream-truncate.txt")
emit writechunk(output, "abcdef") # 6u64
emit truncate(output, 3) # true
emit close(output) # true
emit read("__OSIRIS_DOC_TMP__/stream-truncate.txt") # "abc"

groups.title: Data helpers
groups.summary: Byte work, packing, encoding, and indexable collection helpers.

items.name: bytes
items.summary: Convert values into raw bytes.
details: Use this when you need explicit byte-oriented work rather than text.

items.name: hex
items.summary: Format a value as hexadecimal text.
details: Useful for inspection, logging, and low-level data checks.

items.name: bin
items.summary: Format a value as binary text.
details: Useful for inspection, logging, and bit-level debugging.

items.name: pack
items.summary: Pack structured values into bytes.
details: Useful for binary layouts and compact encoding work.

items.name: unpack
items.summary: Recover values from packed data.
details: This is the inverse of `pack` for supported layouts.

items.name: at
items.summary: Read an element at a given index.
details: Works with byte lists, lists, tensors, and other indexable collections.

items.name: setat
items.summary: Replace an element at a given index.
details: Use this for functional-style updates without mutating the original value.

items.name: encode
items.summary: Serialize an Osiris value.
details: Returns an OSR1 byte string beginning with the four-byte OSR1 header.
Result uses tag 0x16, Option uses tag 0x17, and structured Error uses tag 0x0a with version 1 and the documented field order.
Nested values are bounded by the runtime recursion and 64 MiB resource limits; map keys are encoded in deterministic lexical order.

items.name: decode
items.summary: Restore an Osiris value from encoded bytes.
details: Accepts an OSR1 string or byte-compatible list and validates its header, tags, lengths, presence bytes, recursion depth, and trailing bytes.
The inverse path reconstructs Result, Option, and structured Error values, including nested causes and bounded metadata/stack records.
Decoded storage is owned by the result and is not borrowed from the input byte list.

groups.title: std/crypto
groups.summary: Hashing, mixing, and deterministic noise helpers.

items.name: hash
items.summary: Hash values into a stable text digest.
details: These are the current crypto-flavored helpers exposed through `std/crypto`.
Native C supports SHA-256 `hash` for its parity-tested scalar, string, list, enum, complex, and time value families; other value families remain explicit compile-time boundaries.

The host-independent `hex_encode`, `hex_decode`, and `compare_digest` members have individual interpreter, VM, generated-C, native-executable, ownership, error, and capability evidence. The documented Base64 members remain outside this native slice until their static native admission is added.

items.name: mix
items.summary: Mix values into a deterministic numeric output.
details: Useful for deterministic scramblers and pseudo-random style work.

items.name: noise
items.summary: Generate deterministic noise from inputs.
details: Useful for procedural generation and stable randomized transforms.

items.name: random
items.summary: Generate one deterministic pseudo-random sample from an explicit `seed` and optional sequence `counter`.
details: `random` is pure: it has no process-global state, so the same `seed`/`counter` pair produces the same result in `run` and `vm` regardless of evaluation order.
`counter` defaults to zero and must be a non-negative integer. Increment it explicitly to obtain a reproducible sequence; this helper is not a cryptographic random-number generator.
The explicit-seed form has interpreter, VM, and native C parity for the documented seed and counter types.
items.example:
emit random("osiris", 0)
emit random("osiris", 1)
# Stable distinct f64-backed samples in [0, 1)

groups.title: std/net
groups.summary: Bounded TCP, UDP, DNS, TLS, and HTTP/1.1 host-network resources.

items.name: tcp_listen
items.summary: Bind an owned TCP listener at an explicit address.
details: `address` uses the `host:port` form, including port `0` when the operating system should choose a local port. The caller must `close` the returned listener.
Listening is host I/O and may fail due to permissions or an occupied address. It is interpreter/`vm`-only; native compilation does not support networking.

items.name: tcp_accept
items.summary: Accept one TCP connection as an explicit duplex stream.
details: `timeout_ms` is optional, non-negative, and applies only to this accept call. The result works with `readline`, `readchunk`, `writechunk`, `flush`, and `close`.

Every accepted TCP stream uses the portable low-latency default: `TCP_NODELAY` and keepalive are enabled. The language does not yet expose arbitrary socket options; platform-specific controls remain capability-gated runtime work, not silent behavior.

Accept blocks until a client arrives, the timeout expires, the current task/session is cancelled, or the listener is closed. Closing a listener unblocks its pending accepts but does not close already accepted streams.
A timeout is a `timeout` error; task/session cancellation is a `cancelled` error; a closed local listener is an I/O error. These remain structured errors that `try`/`catch` can inspect.
items.example:
let client = net.tcp_accept(listener, 1000)
writechunk(client, "hello\n")
flush(client)
close(client)

items.name: tcp_dial
items.summary: Connect to one TCP endpoint as an explicit duplex stream.
details: `timeout_ms` is optional and non-negative. A successful connection is a stream; reads observe the current task/session context and stop when it is cancelled or expires.

Every newly dialed TCP stream enables `TCP_NODELAY` and keepalive by default for low-latency request/response traffic. The current language surface intentionally has no raw arbitrary socket-option escape hatch, and native C compilation rejects networking.

Use `close` to release the connection. Connection refusal is `unavailable`, timeout is `timeout`, malformed addresses are `invalid_argument`, and closed local resources are I/O errors; all remain explicit structured errors rather than status values.
items.example:
let peer = net.tcp_dial("127.0.0.1:9000", 1000)
writechunk(peer, "ping\n")
flush(peer)
emit readline(peer)
close(peer)

items.name: udp_bind
items.summary: Create a bounded packet endpoint.
details: `udp_bind` listens at an address and `udp_connect` selects a default peer. `udp_send` accepts byte-compatible data and an optional peer; every packet is bounded to 1 MiB.

The socket is an owned resource. Register `defer { close(socket) }` after acquisition; close is idempotent and interrupts a pending receive. Networking is hosted interpreter/VM I/O and native C reports a source-spanned unsupported diagnostic.

items.name: udp_send
items.syntax: udp_send(socket, data[, peer]) / udp_receive(socket[, max_bytes[, timeout_ms]])
items.summary: Send or receive one bounded UDP datagram.
details: `udp_receive` returns the packet bytes, the sender address, and a truncation flag. A caller should choose a bound larger than the largest expected datagram when an exactly-full packet must be distinguishable from truncation.

Timeouts and task cancellation interrupt the operation and become structured `timeout` or `cancelled` errors. Invalid limits, closed sockets, malformed peers, and packets over the 1 MiB cap fail explicitly.

items.name: dns_lookup
items.summary: Resolve a host under an explicit resolver policy.
details: The optional policy is `system` or `go`; the default is `system`. Results are sorted and duplicate-free so resolver ordering is not observable language state.
The current task context cancels the lookup. Invalid policies and host errors use structured network diagnostics.

items.name: tls_dial
items.syntax: tls_dial(address[, server_name[, timeout_ms]]) / tls_dial_config(address, server_name, roots_pem[, timeout_ms])
items.summary: Open a TLS 1.2-or-newer stream with HTTP/1.1 ALPN.
details: Certificate and hostname verification are always enabled. `tls_dial` uses the platform trust roots; `tls_dial_config` requires a non-empty server name and a caller-supplied PEM root set. There is no insecure-skip-verify option.
The stream uses the normal read/write/flush/close ownership contract. Failed verification, invalid roots, deadlines, cancellation, and connection errors remain structured network errors.

items.name: tls_listen
items.summary: Create a TLS server listener with secure protocol defaults.
details: Certificate and key paths must be absolute. The listener requires TLS 1.2 or newer and advertises only HTTP/1.1 through ALPN.
The returned listener follows the TCP accept and close lifecycle. Native C does not claim host networking support.

items.name: http_get
items.syntax: http_get(url[, timeout_ms]) / http_request(method, url[, headers[, body[, timeout_ms]]])
items.summary: Make a bounded HTTP/1.1 request.
details: Response maps contain `status`, sorted `[name, value]` `headers`, bounded string `body`, and the final `url`. Redirects are limited to five hops; headers are limited to 256 entries and bodies to 8 MiB.

Header names must be valid HTTP token names and values cannot contain control characters or line breaks. Request cancellation and timeout are propagated through the host client. HTTP/2, QUIC, proxy discovery, and decompression are outside this contract.

items.name: http_request_stream
items.summary: Make a bounded request while retaining a streaming response body.
details: The returned `body_stream` remains owned by the caller until `close`; reads are capped at 8 MiB and expose an overflow error rather than silently accepting extra bytes. A stream body supplied as the request is bounded by the same limit.
Close the body stream on every path. The response status, final URL, and deterministic headers are available before the body is consumed.

items.name: http_serve
items.returns: never until cancellation, shutdown, or listener failure
items.summary: Run a cancellable HTTP/1.1 static or dynamic server.
details: The static form serves a bounded body and status. The dynamic form calls `handler(request)` with `method`, `url`, sorted header pairs, bounded `body`, and `remote_addr`; it expects a response map with optional `status`, `headers`, and bounded `body`.

Handlers are serialized per Osiris session so captured state is not concurrently mutated, and background handlers cannot emit. Invalid requests produce 413, handler or response errors produce 500, and cancellation performs graceful shutdown.
items.example:
func handler(request) => { status: 200, headers: {"Content-Type": "text/plain"}, body: "ok" }
http_serve(listener, handler)

groups.title: std/os
groups.summary: Capability-gated command-line, environment, process, signal, and filesystem-watch integration.

legacyItems.name: args
legacyItems.summary: Return deterministic command-line arguments after the executable name.
details: Hosts and tests may inject the argument vector with `Runtime.SetCommandLineArgs`; the returned list is owned and cannot mutate host process state.

legacyItems.name: constants_and_streams
legacyItems.returns: integer constants or owned/borrowed stream values
legacyItems.summary: Expose portable open/seek values, stable error names, the null device, and explicit standard streams.
details: Standard streams are capability-granted borrowed resources; closing them does not close the host descriptor. Raw descriptor access through `fd` requires `os.process_raw_handle`. Unknown or contradictory open flags fail before a host syscall.
legacyItems.example:
import "std/os" as os
emit [os.O_RDONLY, os.SEEK_SET, os.dev_null]

legacyItems.name: env
legacyItems.summary: Read one selected environment variable under the environment capability.
details: The caller must grant `os.environment`. Missing variables return `none()`; values are never included in permission or process diagnostics. Tests can inject an isolated environment.

legacyItems.name: env_names
legacyItems.summary: List selected environment names without exposing their values.
details: Requires `os.environment`; injected environments are sorted lexically for deterministic tests and diagnostics.

legacyItems.name: filesystem
legacyItems.returns: owned file streams, bounded byte lists, metadata maps, or operation status
legacyItems.summary: Open and manipulate files through explicit owned handles and bounded convenience operations.
details: File APIs require the corresponding `os.file_read`, `os.file_write`, `os.file_metadata`, or directory capability. `read_file` is capped at 1 MiB; directory names are sorted; file handles are closed with `close` and compose with `defer`.
`read` and `write` operate on handles, while `read_at`, `write_at`, `seek_file`, `sync`, and `write_string` expose the common Go `File` operations without leaking host descriptors.

legacyItems.name: filesystem_mutation
legacyItems.summary: Mutate paths and inspect links under explicit filesystem capabilities.
details: Mutation is never inferred from an import. `os.file_mutate`, `os.directory_mutate`, and `os.symlink` are separate grants, and fake test runtimes apply the same calls to their in-memory tree.
legacyItems.example:
import "std/os" as os
os.mkdir_all("cache/items", 493)
emit os.read_dir("cache")

legacyItems.name: rooted_filesystem
legacyItems.summary: Create a path-confined root for explicit rooted filesystem operations.
details: Root paths reject lexical traversal outside the selected root, absolute names, NUL bytes, and closed-root access. Derived file handles are invalidated when the root closes. The portable API does not claim resistance to a concurrent symlink swap; deployments requiring that guarantee must use an OS-specific descriptor-relative boundary.

legacyItems.name: test_providers
legacyItems.returns: test status and optional JSON events
legacyItems.summary: Run language source tests with deterministic fake OS providers by default.
details: Each test receives a fresh in-memory filesystem, file-handle, environment, identity, clock, process, and platform provider. Ordinary `std/os` calls use those providers without Go-side registration. Real host access is opt-in through `-integration` and explicit capabilities.

legacyItems.name: environment
legacyItems.returns: Option<string>, sorted list<string>, bool, or string
legacyItems.summary: Read and explicitly mutate the selected process environment.
details: Reads require `os.environment`; mutation requires `os.environment_mutate`. `NewTestRuntime` uses an isolated environment overlay, and host mutation is never performed by import or by ordinary read calls.

legacyItems.name: identity
legacyItems.summary: Read capability-gated host identity and platform-directory information.
details: Identity access requires `os.system_identity`. Test runtimes return deterministic values and do not expose the host account or current directory.

legacyItems.name: process_handles
legacyItems.returns: owned process handle, state map, or bool
legacyItems.summary: Inspect and control process handles with separate capabilities.
details: Process arguments remain shell-free. `process_release` and `close` relinquish owned state; test runtimes use deterministic simulated processes, while real process creation and signaling require explicit grants.

legacyItems.name: process_spawn
legacyItems.returns: map containing an `os_process` and stdin/stdout/stderr streams
legacyItems.summary: Start one child process without invoking a shell.
details: Requires `os.process`. `command` and `arguments` are separate NUL-free strings; the runtime never joins or shell-parses them. Options support `cwd`, an explicit `env` map, and `inherit_env` (false by default).

The returned pipes are owned streams. Child output remains streaming rather than being captured into an unbounded runtime buffer; callers must close every stream and the process, preferably with `defer`.
legacyItems.example: import "std/os" as os; emit os.process_spawn("/bin/echo", ["hello"], { env: { "PATH": "/usr/bin" } })

legacyItems.name: process_wait
legacyItems.returns: map with status, success, and signal
legacyItems.summary: Wait for a child process with an optional timeout.
details: A timeout or task cancellation kills the process group through the platform adapter before returning a structured error. Normal exits return a deterministic status map; non-zero exit status is data rather than an unstructured host error.
legacyItems.example:
import "std/os" as os
# after granting os.process and spawning child:
# emit os.process_wait(child.process, 5000)

legacyItems.name: process_kill
legacyItems.summary: Terminate a child process and its supported process group.
details: Requires `os.process`. Unix adapters use a dedicated process group; Windows and other platforms use their documented direct-process fallback. The operation is idempotent at the language resource boundary.
legacyItems.example:
import "std/os" as os
# after granting os.process and spawning child:
# emit os.process_kill(child.process)

legacyItems.name: signal_subscribe
legacyItems.summary: Subscribe to a supported OS signal as stream notifications.
details: Requires `os.signal`. Names are explicit (`SIGINT`, `SIGTERM`, `SIGHUP`, `SIGUSR1`, and `SIGUSR2` where the platform provides them). Close the stream to unregister; notifications are bounded and dropped rather than allowing unbounded memory growth.
legacyItems.example:
import "std/os" as os
# after granting os.signal:
# emit os.signal_subscribe("SIGTERM")

legacyItems.name: watch
legacyItems.summary: Watch a path through the portable snapshot adapter.
details: Requires `os.watch`. Events are JSON lines with `kind` (`create`, `modify`, `remove`, or `overflow`), normalized slash-separated `path`, and `is_dir` when known. Queue overflow is explicit and requires the caller to rescan. Cancellation and close stop the watcher.
legacyItems.example:
import "std/os" as os
# after granting os.watch:
# emit os.watch("./config", true)

groups.title: std/signal
groups.summary: Deterministic reference signal-processing primitives.

items.name: hann
items.summary: Create a symmetric Hann window.
details: `length` must be a non-negative integer. `hann(0)` is empty and `hann(1)` is `[1]`; longer windows use `0.5 - 0.5*cos(2πi/(length-1))`.
This deterministic scalar reference implementation is shared by `run` and `vm` and has a parity-tested native C lowering. It does not claim SIMD, FFT, GPU, or provider acceleration.
items.example:
import "std/signal" as signal
emit signal.hann(4)
# tensor[4]([0, 0.75, 0.75, 0])

items.name: convolve
items.summary: Compute deterministic full one-dimensional discrete convolution.
details: Both arguments must be rank-one numeric lists or tensors. Empty input produces an empty rank-one `tensor`; invalid rank or non-numeric components fail clearly.

The result uses the full convolution shape. The scalar reference kernel has a parity-tested native C lowering; accelerated backends require separately documented numerical parity and fallback behavior.
items.example:
import "std/signal" as signal
emit signal.convolve([1, 2, 3], [1, 1])
# tensor[4]([1, 3, 5, 3])

groups.title: std/list
groups.summary: Bounded list length, construction, indexing, transforms, grouping, and predicates.

items.name: len
items.summary: Return the length of a collection.
details: These are the smallest `list` utilities and are used throughout examples and tests.

items.name: range
items.summary: Generate a numeric range.
details: Useful for loops, sampling, and numeric iteration.
Native C currently supports the one-argument `range(stop)` form; other `std/list` forms remain compile-time diagnostics.

items.name: take
items.summary: Take the first N values from a collection.
details: Useful for slices, previews, and bounded sampling.

items.name: slice
items.summary: Copy a half-open range from a `tensor`'s leading axis.
details: Without `axis`, `slice` uses the leading axis; `axis` selects any zero-based `tensor` axis.
The result preserves its other dimensions and owns its data. Bounds are non-negative; endpoints above the selected dimension are clamped, while `end` before `start` is an error.

items.name: sum
items.summary: Reduce a collection by addition.
details: This is the standard additive reducer for numeric collections.

items.name: product
items.summary: Reduce a collection by multiplication.
details: This is the standard multiplicative reducer for numeric collections.

items.name: reverse
items.summary: Return a reversed copy of a list.
details: The source list is not mutated and the result owns its element array.

items.name: at
items.summary: Read one zero-based list element.
details: The index must be a non-negative integer in range; invalid access returns a structured error.

items.name: index_of
items.summary: Return the first matching index or -1.
details: Equality follows the language value comparison contract and the input remains unchanged.

items.name: last_index_of
items.summary: Return the last matching index or -1.
details: The search is deterministic and bounded by the list item limit.

items.name: contains
items.summary: Test whether a list contains a value.
details: The scan short-circuits on the first equal element and allocates no result list.

items.name: count
items.summary: Count equal values in a list.
details: The bounded equality scan returns an unsigned count without mutating the source.

items.name: sort
items.summary: Return a stable ascending copy.
details: Values must be mutually orderable; incomparable values return a structured error and the input remains unchanged.

items.name: unique
items.summary: Remove duplicates while preserving first occurrence order.
details: The result is independently owned and uses the shared equality contract.

items.name: chunks
items.summary: Split a list into fixed-width chunks.
details: `values` is bounded and `width` is a positive integer no greater than the list item limit.
Each chunk owns a copied element array, the final chunk may be shorter, and invalid input produces a structured error without mutating the source or requiring a host capability.

items.name: zip
items.summary: Pair values at matching positions.
details: The result stops at the shorter list and each pair is a tuple with newly owned storage.

items.name: concat
items.summary: Concatenate zero or more lists.
details: The total result size is checked before allocation and inputs are never mutated.

items.name: repeat
items.summary: Create count copies of a value.
details: Count must be non-negative and within the list item bound; allocation happens only after validation.

items.name: empty
items.summary: Create an empty list.
details: The result is a pure owned value and the function accepts no arguments.

items.name: all
items.summary: Test whether every list value is truthy.
details: Empty input returns true and evaluation short-circuits on the first false value.
items.example:
import "std/list" as list
emit list.all([true, true])

items.name: any
items.summary: Test whether any list value is truthy.
details: Empty input returns false and evaluation short-circuits on the first true value.
items.example:
import "std/list" as list
emit list.any([false, true])

items.name: none
items.summary: Test whether no list value is truthy.
details: Empty input returns true and evaluation stops at the first true value.
items.example:
import "std/list" as list
emit list.none([false, false])

items.name: enumerate
items.summary: Pair each value with its zero-based index.
details: Pairs are emitted in source order and each pair is represented as a tuple.
